lesson.text: Quick memory: is a microphone an input or an output? (An input: sound goes into the computer.) Today: inside the computer, and the software that runs it.
The processor (CPU) is the computer's brain. It fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it (works out what it means) and executes it, billions of times a second.
Memory (RAM) holds the programs and data in use right now. It is very fast, but it forgets everything when the power goes off.
Storage, like a solid-state drive, keeps files when the power is off: photos, programs and saved worlds. It is slower than memory but holds far more.
Sizes: 8 bits make a byte. 1,000 bytes make a kilobyte (KB), 1,000 KB make a megabyte (MB) and 1,000 MB make a gigabyte (GB). A photo might be 4 MB.
Software is the programs. The operating system runs the whole computer: it starts programs, shares out the memory, looks after files and talks to the hardware. Apps like this game run on top of it.
Worked example: you tap PLAY. The tap is input; the operating system passes it to the game; the processor runs the game's code from memory; your world loads from storage onto the screen.
Try it in the world: with a grown-up, look in a computer's or tablet's settings for its processor, memory and storage sizes. Next: spreadsheet models.

exercises.prompt: Which part is the computer's brain, following the instructions?
exercises.explain: The processor (CPU) carries out the instructions.

exercises.prompt: Memory (RAM) keeps your files when the computer is switched off.
exercises.hint: What happens to RAM when the power goes?
exercises.explain: False: RAM forgets when the power goes off; storage keeps files.

exercises.hint: Software is programs; hardware is parts you can touch.
exercises.explain: The operating system is a program: software.

exercises.hint: Can you touch it? Then it is hardware.
exercises.explain: Hardware: processor, keyboard, memory chips. Software: a game, the operating system, a painting app.

exercises.prompt: Label the inside of the computer: tap a word, then its number.
exercises.hint: The processor is a square chip; memory is sticks; storage is a drive; the power supply has a fan.
exercises.explain: The square chip is the processor, the two sticks are memory, the drive is storage and the fan box is the power supply.

exercises.prompt: Put the processor's cycle in order.
exercises.hint: It must get the instruction before it can understand it.
items: decode it (work out what it means)

exercises.prompt: How many bits are in 4 bytes?
Why does a computer have both memory and storage?
exercises.hint: Which one forgets when the power goes? Which is faster?
choices: memory is fast for now; storage keeps things
exercises.explain: Memory is fast but forgets; storage is slower but keeps your files.

exercises.prompt: Match each part to its job.
exercises.explain: The processor runs instructions, memory holds what is in use, storage keeps files and the operating system runs the whole computer.

exercises.prompt: Which is a job of the operating system?
exercises.hint: It manages the computer for all the programs.
choices: sharing out the memory between programs
exercises.explain: The operating system shares out memory, starts programs and looks after files.

exercises.prompt: A 2 GB memory card holds how many 4 MB photos? (1 GB is 1,000 MB.)
exercises.hint: Change GB into MB, then share by 4.
The ports are on the board's edge, where cables plug in.
exercises.explain: The fan box is the power supply, the square chip the processor, the sticks memory, the drive storage, and the sockets on the edge are ports.

exercises.prompt: Adding more memory (RAM) can help a computer run more programs at once.
exercises.hint: Where do programs sit while they run?
exercises.explain: True: running programs sit in memory, so more of it holds more at once.

exercises.prompt: A processor does 3 billion steps a second. How many billion steps does it do in 5 seconds?
exercises.hint: Multiply the steps in one second by the seconds.

exercises.prompt: A game saves your world when you quit. Where is it kept?
exercises.hint: It must still be there after the power goes off.
exercises.explain: Storage keeps it with the power off, ready next time.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: does it forget when the power goes, or keep its data?
exercises.hint: Careful: a name can trick you. What does each do when the power goes off?
exercises.explain: Only RAM forgets. A memory card is storage, despite its name: it keeps photos with no power.
